name: Glass Refraction
basis: why: glass bends light, ribs squeeze and mirror slices, beads invert, dispersion fringes; how: per-pixel refracted lookup per lens
note: Models the optics of reeded glass, beads and bubbles, not how the glass is made.

lumenary.blurb: Your picture seen through ribbed glass, glass beads or soap bubbles, each splitting a little colour at the edges.

facts.era: Optics theory 10th and 17th centuries, reeded glass in 20th century design
facts.bestOn: Pictures with clear colours and strong shapes

why: Glass bends light, so what you see through it comes from somewhere else. Ribs squeeze and mirror slices of the scene, beads show tiny upside-down copies, and bubbles magnify their middles. Because glass bends blue more than red, each colour channel is bent a little differently and edges pick up coloured fringes.
how: For each output pixel decide where in the picture to look, and take that colour.
For ribbed glass, run the sampling point across a wider part of the picture than the rib itself, and backwards, so each rib shows a squeezed, mirrored slice.
For beads, do the same in two directions on a hexagonal grid. For bubbles, magnify the middle of each disc.
Sample the three colour channels with slightly different strengths for the coloured fringes.
Shade each lens with a darker rim and a small bright window reflection, drawing lenses one at a time inside their bounding boxes.
history: The law of refraction was written down by Ibn Sahl around 984 and rediscovered by Willebrord Snell in the early 1600s. Isaac Newton showed in 1666 that a prism splits white light into colours. Fluted and reeded glass became a favourite of Art Deco interiors and returned as a popular detail in modern homes and shops.
terms: The bending of light as it passes from one material into another.
Different colours bending by different amounts, which splits white light.
A shaped piece of glass that bends light to focus or spread it.
paragraphs: Glass bends light, so what you see through it comes from somewhere else. For every output pixel the program decides where in the picture to look, and takes that colour instead. Ribbed glass is a row of cylinder lenses: within each rib the sampling point runs across a wider part of the picture than the rib itself, and backwards, so each rib shows a squeezed, mirrored slice of the scene. Glass beads are tiny spheres on a hexagonal grid doing the same in two directions, and the sheet between them is dark. Bubbles are the opposite kind of lens: they magnify the middle of the disc, because the sampling radius is smaller than the pixel’s own radius.

Glass bends blue more than red, so the three colour channels are each sampled with a slightly different strength, which gives coloured fringes. Each lens is also shaded: beads are darker toward the rim, both kinds get a small bright window reflection at the top left, and bubbles get a thin ring of light at the edge. Lenses are drawn one at a time inside their bounding boxes (largest bubble first), so the cost is the area of the lenses, not of lenses times pixels.

equations.note: Ribbed glass: x₀ is the rib centre, u from −1 to 1 the position in the rib, w its width, β the bend slider, δ = 0.1 × the colour-split slider.
Glass bead: n is the pixel’s position in the bead (−1 to 1), R its radius; the minus sign inverts the image.
Bubble: a pixel at radius ρ looks at radius ρ^e, nearer the centre, so the middle is magnified.

presets.text: Wide ribs with strong bend look like a shower screen.
Tiny beads turn the picture into a glittering mosaic.
Bubbles with a strong colour split look like soap film.
